title: CDC: Information for Clinicians
text:
## Information for Clinicians
## At a glance
Work-related asthma includes occupational asthma and work-exacerbated asthma. Occupational asthma is new onset asthma caused by exposures at work. Work-exacerbated asthma is previously diagnosed asthma that gets worse at work. Clinicians should consider work-related asthma anytime a patient is experiencing new or worsening symptoms.
## Pathophysiology
Signs and symptoms of work-related asthma are generally the same as those of non-work-related asthma. Work-related asthma is caused or worsened by exposure to:
- Sensitizers
- Irritants
- Physical conditions

title: CDC: Information for Clinicians
text:
## Sensitizers
Sensitizers are agents that initiate an allergic (immunologic) response. There is typically a latency period of at least a few months between first exposure and becoming sensitized. Sensitizers are divided into high-molecular weight and low-molecular weight agents:
- High-molecular-weight agents: (e.g., cereals, coffee beans, enzymes, flour, grain dust, plant proteins, seafood, latex, wood dust) stimulate production of specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies. During re-exposure, the agent cross-links specific antibodies on mast cells and activates them to release inflammatory mediators leading to asthma symptoms.
- Low-molecular-weight agents: (e.g., acrylates, anhydrides, diisocyanates, dyes, formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, metals, persulfates) are incomplete antigens, called haptens, that often combine with a protein to produce a sensitizing agent.

title: CDC: Information for Clinicians
text:
## Irritants
- Induce a non-allergic response and include gases, fumes, vapors, and aerosols.
- Non-allergen-induced asthma pathophysiology is less understood.
## Physical conditions
- Exposure to cold air and physical exertion.
- Cooling or drying of the airway is thought to lead to bronchoconstriction.
Regardless of the asthma trigger type, the response is characterized by inflammation, edema, bronchoconstriction, and buildup of mucus in the airways. This leads to coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.

title: CDC: Center for Work and Fatigue Research
text:
## Center for Work and Fatigue Research
## Key points
- Committed to exploring and mitigating health and safety risks related to nonstandard work schedules and worker fatigue.
- Aims to develop and implement effective solutions and strategies for managing workplace fatigue.
- Engages in active collaboration with researchers, policymakers, employers, workers, and health and safety professionals.

title: CDC: Center for Work and Fatigue Research
text:
## Overview
The Center for Work and Fatigue Research (CWFR) is dedicated to expanding work on health and safety risks associated with nonstandard work schedules and other sources of fatigue. The Center seeks to develop practical and effective solutions to these challenges.
Fatigue has been described as "a feeling of weariness, tiredness or lack of energy." In workplace settings, it is commonly associated with nonstandard schedules which disrupt or shorten sleep. Examples of nonstandard schedules include night shift work and extended work hours. Nearly 30% of the American workforce has a work schedule that is outside of a "regular daytime shift." One in four workers reports working more than 40 hours per week. Fatigue can also be associated with other workplace factors. Learn more on the NIOSH fatigue worker safety and health topic page .

title: CDC: Center for Work and Fatigue Research
text:
## Program priorities
The Center for Work and Fatigue Research launched in May 2020. The CFWR collaborates with other government agencies, industry, labor, safety professionals, and scientific researchers. Through these partnerships, the Center aims to:
- Raise awareness of various sources of worker fatigue
- Identify effective methods to assess fatigue-risk in workplaces
- Reduce health and safety risks associated with workplace fatigue

title: CDC: Center for Work and Fatigue Research
text:
## What we've accomplished
- Hosted a mini symposium on work-related fatigue for the NIOSH Board of Scientific Counselors in May 2021. Presentation topics included the evolution of fatigue research, COVID-19 and work-related fatigue, fatigue risk management strategies and global perspectives of work-related fatigue.
- Published science blogs on shift work, fatigue, and fatigue detection technologies.
- Published an article proposing an industrial hygiene approach to anticipate, recognize, evaluate, and control work-related fatigue.
- Contributed articles to the American Journal of Industrial Medicine about current knowledge and gaps in work-related fatigue research and effective countermeasures.Topics include: mining , oil and gas extraction , economic benefits and cost , and populations at disproportionate risks .

title: CDC: Center for Work and Fatigue Research
text:
- Conducted a systematic review of fatigue interventions used in mining operations and similar industries. Substantial evidence was found for the use of bright-light treatments to improve night shift worker alertness.
- Reviewed and validated data for World Health Organization/International Labour Organization study: Burden of ischemic heart disease and stroke attributable to long work hours for 194 countries: 2000-2016 . Working 55 or more hours per week had a higher risk of stroke and dying from ischemic heart disease compared to working 35-40 hours per week.
- Presented on the benefits and challenges of fatigue detection technologies at the Electric Power Research Institute Thought Leadership webinar series, NIOSH Data 2 Info Workshop , National Safety Council Work to Zero meeting, OSHA Oil and Gas Conference and XXII World Congress on Safety and Health at Work

title: CDC: Center for Work and Fatigue Research
text: - Developed the infographic "How to Choose the Right Fatigue Detection Technology for Your Workplace" to highlight factors for employers to consider when selecting a technologies as part of a comprehensive safety management system.

title: CDC: Center for Work and Fatigue Research
text:
## What's ahead
- Publish a Cochrane Review on adaptation of shift work schedules to reduce sleepiness and improve sleep.
- Develop videos with tips to manage fatigue during challenging times.
- Publish a scoping review of sleep education and training interventions for nurses.
- Partner with US Department of Transportation, Volpe Center, to develop communication and educational products about risk of fatigue with automated and assisted driving.
- Publish a thematic journal issue of emerging concerns in workplace fatigue and effective solutions specific to various industry sectors.

For more information or inquiries about the Center's initiatives, contact the Center for Work and Fatigue Research at cwfr@cdc.gov .

title: CDC: Preventing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Preventing Work-related Asthma
## What to know
Minimizing exposure to work-related asthma triggers can help employees to be healthier. The following guidelines can help employers and employees develop and maintain a worksite safe from asthma triggers.

title: CDC: Preventing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Employer
The hierarchy of controls is a multi-faceted approach to eliminate or reduce workplace hazards. This approach includes the following:
- Eliminate hazardous processes or materials from work tasks.
- Substitute by using less hazardous processes or materials.
- Install engineering controls. Examples include isolating or enclosing processes or installing local exhaust ventilation.
- Implement administrative controls such as work practices, policies, and worker training.
- Personal protective equipment (PPE) such as respiratory protection.
PPE should not be the sole method for protecting workers. Eliminate, substitute, and use effective engineering and administrative controls together with PPE.

title: CDC: Preventing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Medical surveillance
Some employers might want to consider establishing a medical surveillance plan to monitor workers for asthma. Medical surveillance plans can help identify workers with asthma at earlier stages of disease. This can eliminate workers from exposure and prevent disease progression. Surveillance can be as simple as periodically completing a questionnaire. Plans should also include:
- Periodic screening of workers for symptoms of asthma
- Follow up medical testing when appropriate
Additional testing, such as evaluating for sensitization with allergy skin tests, has also been used.
If there is not an established medical surveillance program, consider consulting with an occupational physician to discuss monitoring options.

title: CDC: Preventing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Employees
Employees should pay attention to their work environment, especially those with breathing problems. Follow the steps below if you feel you have work-related asthma symptoms.
- Identify and avoid exposures to asthma triggers.
- Participate in your employer's asthma surveillance plan, if available.
- Report new or worsening breathing problems to your doctor and the designated person at your workplace.
- Report if personal protective equipment or engineering controls malfunction to your supervisor or designated person.
- If you have asthma, take your medications as prescribed and regularly see your doctor.
- Get a flu shot every year and stay up to date with COVID-19 vaccines.
- If you smoke, talk to your doctor or employer about resources to help you quit smoking .

text:

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
## At a glance
Diagnosing work-related asthma is based on a combination of medical and exposure history, physical examination, and medical tests such as pulmonary function tests.
## Considerations
Consider work-related asthma as a possibility in all working patients. This includes those with new onset asthma or asthma that clinically worsens after previously being controlled.
Ask patients screening questions about their working conditions. If their answers suggest a connection, obtain a comprehensive work history. The work history should include:
- Current and past job titles
- Job descriptions
- Known exposure

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Examples of work history questions
- What kind of work do you do?
- Are you now or have you previously been exposed to dust, fumes, or chemicals at your workplace?
- Are your respiratory symptoms better or worse when away from work, such as on weekends or vacation?
- Do you think your health problems are related to your work?
An electronic occupational exposure history form is available at the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) website .
## Evaluate symptoms and work schedules
- Symptoms can occur at work in response to an exposure or can be delayed (occurring several hours after work).
- Symptoms of severe work-related asthma might not improve away from work for a work-related pattern to be evident.
## Document changes in medication
An increase in using rescue inhalers can be an early indication that asthma is progressing.

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Document changes in medication
An increase in using rescue inhalers can be an early indication that asthma is progressing.
## Physical examination
- Exam findings are typically non-specific.
- Patients with asthma often have normal physical examinations between asthma attacks.
- If wheezing is present, it is generally on expiration. However, sometimes wheezing might also be auscultated on inspiration.
## Temporary work furlough
A short period away from work period can help diagnose patients you suspect have work-related asthma. When away, improvements in pulmonary function tests such as ambulatory peak expiratory flow or bronchial responsiveness measured by methacholine challenge support an occupational etiology.

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Differential diagnosis
Some health conditions have symptoms similar to asthma. In adults, the differential diagnosis of asthma includes, but is not limited to, the following:
- Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
- Non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis
- Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
- Vocal cord dysfunction
- Obliterative bronchiolitis
## Medical tests
## Pulmonary function tests
The American Thoracic Society has guidelines on how to perform and interpret pulmonary function tests such as spirometry.

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Pulmonary function tests
The American Thoracic Society has guidelines on how to perform and interpret pulmonary function tests such as spirometry.
## Peak expiratory flow
Serial measurements of peak expiratory flow might be useful for evaluating work-related asthma. Provide instructions to the patient on how to use a peak flow meter (spirometer). Ask the patient to record their peak expiratory flow:
- Four times a day on when off work
- On workdays (before, during and after work)
- Before going to bed every day
Record measurements in a journal or diary over several weeks for best interpretations. Many spirometers automatically record measurements with date and time information. This can be downloaded from a clinical office for review.

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Bronchodilator reversibility testing for spirometry
When spirometry results show a patient has airways obstruction, the next step is to assess reversibility with an inhaled bronchodilator. The presence of reversibility may support an asthma diagnosis.
## Nonspecific bronchial responsiveness (bronchoprovocation testing)
If spirometry is normal but asthma is suspected, bronchial hyperresponsiveness can be assessed using nonspecific bronchial responsive testing (e.g., methacholine or mannitol challenge tests).

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Exhaled nitric oxide
- Fractional exhaled nitric oxide is a marker of allergic airways inflammation.
- The American Thoracic Society has guidelines on how to measure and interpret exhaled nitric oxide levels.
- Increased fractional exhaled nitric oxide levels support allergic asthma diagnosis but does not differentiate between work-related asthma and non-work related.
- A normal fractional exhaled nitric oxide level does not rule out work-related asthma.

title: CDC: Diagnosing Work-related Asthma
text:
## Other tests
- Serologic testing to measure IgE antibodies for specific allergens.
- Skin prick, patch, or intradermal testing to look for allergic reactions to specific substances.
Some medical conditions can make asthma worse. Additionally, other tests are needed to evaluate for gastroesophogeal reflux and rhinosinusitis.

title: CDC: Treating Work-related Asthma
text:
## Treating Work-related Asthma
## At a glance
The two most important factors for managing work-related asthma are avoiding environmental triggers and medically controlling clinical symptoms. This page provides guidance on treatment options.
## Treatment
## Avoid allergens and irritants
Reduce occupational and environmental exposures. Reduce occupational and environmental exposures to allergens, irritants, and physical conditions known to worsen asthma symptoms.
Smoking cessation. If relevant, initiate a smoking cessation program. Smoking has been associated with difficulty controlling asthma.
Refer to a specialist. Consider referring to a pulmonary, allergy, or occupational medicine specialist to further test and identify work-related exposures.

title: CDC: Treating Work-related Asthma
text:
## Work modification or restrictions
Eliminate exposures. Eliminating exposures is the best approach for workers with work-related asthma. Reducing exposures by using workplace controls may also benefit workers.
Individualized management plan. For some workers, an individualized management plan is required. This depends on medical findings and response to reducing allergens and irritants. An example includes assigning an affected employee to a different location away from triggers.
## Medication
The Global Initiative for Asthma provides a stepwise approach to pharmacologic therapy. Also, immunizations such as pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccines are recommended.

title: CDC: Treating Work-related Asthma
text:
## Workplace assessment
Review copies of the Safety Data Sheets (SDS). These sheets can help identify potential work-related asthma triggers. The employer should be able to provide copies. The Association of Occupational and Environmental Clinics has a tool to help healthcare providers determine if substances are known asthmagens.
Contact employee/occupational health or an industrial hygiene specialist. Conduct workplace assessments for potential allergens, irritants, and harmful physical conditions.
Discuss NIOSH's Health Hazard Evaluation (HHE) Program with patients. This program offers free and confidential assistance with identifying worksite asthma triggers.

## Haemophilus influenzae Disease Surveillance and Trends
## Key points
- CDC tracks invasive Haemophilus influenzae disease using 2 surveillance systems.
- Invasive disease refers to when bacteria invade parts of the body, like blood, that are normally free from germs.
- CDC doesn't track non-invasive H. influenzae disease, such as ear infections.
- Learn about the latest trends in invasive H. influenzae disease.
## Data systems
## National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System
Invasive H. influenzae disease is a nationally notifiable disease .
CDC collects national information about invasive H. influenzae disease through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS). CDC receives NNDSS data each week.

title: CDC: Haemophilus influenzae Disease Surveillance and Trends
text:
## Active Bacterial Core surveillance
CDC also collects information from laboratories in 10 areas of the country through Active Bacterial Core surveillance (ABCs). ABCs is part of CDC's Emerging Infections Program .
## Bact Facts Interactive
## How the data are interpreted
## Disease trends
The epidemiology of invasive H. influenzae disease has changed since the United States began using Hib vaccines. Hib vaccination began for children in 1987 and for infants in 1990.
Since then, the annual incidence of invasive disease in children younger than 5 years old has changed:
- Type b: Decreased by 99%
- Non-b: Increasing (primarily types a and f)
- Nontypeable: Increasing

title: CDC: About Haemophilus influenzae Disease
text:
## About Haemophilus influenzae Disease
## Key points
- Bacteria called Haemophilus influenzae can cause many types of infections.
- Some of these infections are mild, while others are serious.
- Despite its name, H. influenzae doesn't cause the flu.
- Learn about how vaccines can prevent infections from one type of H. influenzae , type b or Hib.
## What it is
H. influenzae disease is a name for any infection caused by H. influenzae bacteria.
## Types
H. influenzae can cause many different types of infections. These infections range from mild, like ear infections, to serious, like bloodstream infections.

title: CDC: About Haemophilus influenzae Disease
text:
## Serious infections
The most common serious infections caused by H. influenzae are:
- Pneumonia (a lung infection)
- Bloodstream infection
- Meningitis (swelling of the lining of the brain and spinal cord)
- Epiglottitis (swelling of the throat)
- Cellulitis (skin infection)
- Infectious arthritis (swelling of a joint)
## Mild infections
H. influenzae are a common cause of ear infections in children and bronchitis (chest cold) in adults.
## Symptoms
H. influenzae can cause many different types of infections. Symptoms depend on the part of the body that's infected. Serious infections can result in long-term health problems and death.
## Risk factors
People of certain ages and racial or ethnic groups are at increased risk for H. influenzae disease. Some medical conditions can also increase someone's risk.

title: CDC: About Haemophilus influenzae Disease
text:
## Causes
H. influenzae are bacteria that live in people's nose and throat. Usually, these bacteria cause no harm. However, they can move to other parts of the body and cause infection.
## Did you know?
## Spread to others
People spread H. influenzae to others by coughing or sneezing , which creates small respiratory droplets that contain the bacteria. Other people can get infected if they breathe in those droplets.
People who aren't sick but have the bacteria in their nose and throat can still spread the bacteria. That's how H. influenzae spreads most of the time.
The bacteria can also spread to people who have close or lengthy contact with a person with H. influenzae disease.

title: CDC: About Haemophilus influenzae Disease
text:
## Prevention
People can get H. influenzae , including Hib, disease more than once. Maintaining healthy habits helps prevent H. influenzae disease. Examples of healthy habits include washing hands often and not having close contact with people who are sick.
## Vaccination
Vaccines can prevent Hib disease, but not disease caused by other H. influenzae . The best way to prevent Hib disease is to get vaccinated. CDC recommends Hib vaccines for all children younger than 5 years old.
## Antibiotics
Sometimes close contacts of someone with Hib disease should receive antibiotics to prevent them from getting sick. A healthcare provider or health department generally decides who should get preventive antibiotics.
## Testing and diagnosis
Healthcare providers usually diagnose H. influenzae disease with one or more lab tests . The most common testing methods use a sample of blood or spinal fluid.

title: CDC: About Haemophilus influenzae Disease
text:
## Treatment and recovery
People diagnosed with H. influenzae disease take antibiotics to treat the infection.
People with serious infections may need care in a hospital. Other treatments may include:
- Breathing support
- Medicine to treat low blood pressure
- Wound care for parts of the body with damaged skin

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text:
## Summary
What is already known about this topic?
Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in approximately 20% of hospitalized adults and is associated with higher risk for long-term chronic kidney disease, kidney failure, and death. AKI can occur after a drug overdose, but national data on AKI in drug overdose–involved hospitalizations remain limited.
What is added by this report?
Analysis of 2016–2025 hospital discharge data found that AKI occurred in approximately one third of drug overdose–involved hospitalizations; of those, approximately two thirds involved a severe inpatient course. AKI incidence was higher with older age, but severe inpatient courses among AKI cases were lower with older age. Among patients with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations, AKI increased during 2016–2022 and decreased during 2022–2025.
What are the implications for public health practice?

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text:
What are the implications for public health practice?
Because the exposure is identifiable and potentially avoidable, some drug overdose–related AKI might be preventable. Clinician awareness and overdose prevention efforts can help reduce AKI and prevent long-term kidney complications.

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious, often underrecognized complication among patients hospitalized for drug overdose. Although overdose mortality has recently declined in the United States, less is known about whether serious nonfatal complications, including AKI, have followed similar trends. Adjusted percentages of hospitalizations of patients with drug overdose and AKI were calculated using hospital discharge data during 2016–2025. The percentage with a severe inpatient course (i.e., acute dialysis, respiratory compromise, shock or hypotension, or in-hospital death) was also calculated. Among 1,297,847 drug overdose–involved hospitalizations, AKI was documented in 448,136 (34.5%). The percentage of patients with AKI was 28.2% among those aged ≤24 years, 37.4% among those aged ≥65 years, 29.4% among females, and 38.1% among males

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . AKI among patients with a drug overdose–involved hospitalization increased during 2016–2022 (annual percent change [APC] = 2.69%) and decreased during 2022–2025 (APC = −5.11%). Among patients with a drug overdose–involved hospitalization and AKI, 273,093 (60.9%) experienced a severe inpatient course, including 68.1% of persons aged ≤24 years, 56.1% of those aged ≥65 years, 61.9% of females, and 60.4% of males. The percentage of drug overdose–involved hospitalizations with a severe inpatient course increased during 2016–2023 (APC = 1.82%), before decreasing during 2023–2025 (APC = −2.89%)

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . Disproportionately severe inpatient courses among younger patients, who might have more years of life at risk for developing chronic kidney disease or kidney failure after AKI, warrants continued attention to early kidney injury detection after drug overdose, postdischarge linkage to care, and overdose prevention through improved access to substance use treatment.

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text:
## Introduction
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious in-hospital complication occurring in approximately 20% of hospitalized adults and is associated with higher risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD), kidney failure, and death. In addition, AKI is associated with substantial health care costs, including an estimated $1,795 increase in cost per hospitalization compared with admissions without AKI, and $11,016 in additional costs per hospitalization when dialysis is required ( 1 , 2 ).

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: Traditional overdose surveillance has primarily focused on fatal overdoses and nonfatal overdose-related emergency department visits . Less is known about serious inpatient complications, including AKI, that might contribute to adverse longer-term health outcomes. Although AKI occurs across hospitalizations for a wide range of conditions, drug overdose–related AKI might warrant separate consideration because it typically follows an identifiable, potentially preventable exposure. Whereas many established risk factors for AKI, including older patient age and the presence of preexisting cardiovascular comorbidities, are not readily modifiable ( 1 ), the risk for drug overdose–related AKI might be mitigated through early recognition and reduction of substance exposure ( 3 ).

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: AKI can arise through various mechanisms after a drug overdose, including rhabdomyolysis, ischemic injury, and substance-specific nephrotoxicity, which vary by substance type ( 3 ). Although acute renal failure was reported in 33% of patients hospitalized for cocaine intoxication with rhabdomyolysis ( 4 ), national trends in coexisting AKI among drug overdose–involved hospitalizations, including demographic patterns and drug overdose AKI–associated inpatient severity, remain poorly characterized. Quantifying the prevalence of AKI among patients with a drug overdose–involved hospitalization and the percentage of these hospitalizations with a severe inpatient course could help identify groups at high risk for complications and guide the development and implementation of prevention and clinical management strategies aimed at reducing overdose-related AKI morbidity and health care costs

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . This report assessed trends in AKI among patients with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations during 2016–2025 and examined trends in severe inpatient courses among patients with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations and AKI.

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text:
## Data Sources
The 2016–2025 hospital discharges recorded by the Premier Healthcare Database (PHD), a large hospital-based, all-payer, service-level database, were analyzed. PHD includes data from approximately 1,400 hospitals and health care systems, representing approximately 25% of annual U.S. inpatient admissions.

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: This analysis focused on selected substance-specific overdose hospitalizations involving opioids, cocaine, or psychostimulants, drug categories that are commonly involved in U.S. overdose deaths ( 5 ). A hospitalization for drug overdose* was defined as a patient admission with an International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification ( ICD-10-CM ) diagnosis code indicating opioid, cocaine, or psychostimulant poisoning in any diagnosis field and coded as present on admission. Among drug overdose–involved hospitalizations, those of patients with AKI † were identified by the presence of AKI in any diagnosis field. Among drug overdose–involved hospitalizations of patients with AKI, patients who received acute dialysis or experienced respiratory compromise, shock or hypotension, or who died while hospitalized were classified as having a severe inpatient course

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: Annual percentages of drug overdose–involved hospitalizations of patients with AKI were estimated. Among patients with an overdose-involved hospitalization and AKI, the percentages of hospitalizations in which patients experienced severe inpatient courses were also estimated. For both outcomes, 95% CIs were obtained from weighted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for discharge year (categorical), age group, sex, race and ethnicity, CKD, heart failure, liver disease, diabetes, and type of drug involved in the overdose. ¶ Estimates by age group and sex were derived from models with interactions between year and the respective subgroup, adjusting for the remaining covariates. Pooled 2016–2025 adjusted percentages were estimated overall and by age group and by sex using the same covariates but without year-by-subgroup interaction terms

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . Joinpoint regression (with a maximum of 1 joinpoint for 10 data points) was used to estimate annual percentage changes (APC). Inpatient projection weights provided by PHD were applied to generate national weighted estimates of hospitalizations, and variance estimation accounted for clustering at the hospital level. The unit of analysis was a hospitalization; therefore, an individual patient could contribute more than one hospitalization included, and patient characteristics such as age and sex were those documented for each hospitalization rather than for unique patients. Analyses were conducted using Azure Databricks (version 4.5.0 R, Microsoft Azure), and Joinpoint software (version 6.0.1; National Cancer Institute). This activity was reviewed by CDC, deemed not research, and conducted consistent with applicable federal law and CDC policy.**

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text:
## Results
## Percentage and Characteristics of Patients with AKI and Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations
Overall, among 1,297,847 drug overdose–involved hospitalizations during 2016–2025, AKI was reported among 448,136 (34.5%) hospitalized patients. The percentage of drug overdose–involved hospitalizations with AKI was higher among older patients, ranging from 28.2% among patients aged ≤24 years to 37.4% among those aged ≥65 years (p-value <0.001) and was lower among females (29.4%) than among males (38.1%) (p-value <0.001) ( Table 1 ). The percentage of patients with AKI increased during 2016–2022 (APC = 2.69%; 95% CI = 1.79%–3.65%), then decreased during 2022–2025 (APC = −5.11%) ( Table 2 ).

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text:
## Percentage and Characteristics of Severe Inpatient Course Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved AKI Hospitalizations
Among the 448,136 drug overdose–involved hospitalizations of patients with AKI during 2016–2025, 273,093 (60.9%) involved a severe inpatient course. This percentage was lower with older patient age, ranging from a high of 68.1% among patients aged ≤24 years to 56.1% among those aged ≥65 years (p-value <0.001) and was higher among females (61.9%) than among males (60.4%) (p-value <0.001) (Table 1). The percentage of a severe inpatient course increased during 2016–2023 (APC = 1.82%), then decreased during 2023–2025 (APC = −2.89%) (Table 2).

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text:
## Temporal Trends by Demographic Subgroups
Temporal patterns across demographic subgroups generally followed the overall trend of an initial increase followed by a decline, with both APCs statistically significant in all subgroups ( Figure ), except that the decline in severe inpatient course was not statistically significant among patients aged ≤24 and 25–44 years or among females (Table 2). In age subgroup analyses, opposing age gradients were observed: whereas the percentage of drug overdose–involved hospitalizations with AKI was higher with older age, the percentage of those hospitalizations with AKI with a severe inpatient course was lower among older patients throughout the study period.

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: This analysis characterized the percentage of drug overdose–involved hospitalizations with AKI and the severe inpatient course among patients with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations and AKI, highlighting kidney injury as an important component of overdose-related morbidity. The findings suggest that AKI occurrence in drug overdose–involved hospitalizations was higher among older patients and was more common among males, whereas severe inpatient course was more common among younger age groups and among females. Older age is a known risk factor for AKI ( 1 ), consistent with the finding that AKI occurred more frequently among older patients

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . Older age is a known risk factor for AKI ( 1 ), consistent with the finding that AKI occurred more frequently among older patients. In contrast, the percentage of patients with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations and AKI who experienced a severe inpatient course was highest among persons aged ≤24 years, which might partly reflect age-related differences in the types of illicit drugs involved across age groups. Among patients hospitalized with rhabdomyolysis, illicit drug use has been associated with younger age, more severe AKI, and the need for dialysis ( 6 ).

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: The percentage of males with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations who experienced AKI was consistently higher than that of females in this study population; this finding aligns with recent inpatient opioid overdose literature reporting lower adjusted odds of AKI among females ( 7 ). However, when AKI did occur, the percentage of severe inpatient course was slightly higher among females than among males. A previous study reported that female sex and the occurrence of shock or hypotension were risk factors for severe opioid-related adverse events among hospitalized patients ( 8 ); however, evidence of sex-specific patterns of hemodynamic instability in patients with drug overdose–related AKI remains limited.

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: Drug overdose–involved AKI should be considered both an acute inpatient complication and a marker of long-term risk for CKD. Because AKI is associated with subsequent CKD and kidney failure ( 1 ), the frequency of severe inpatient course among persons aged ≤24 years is particularly concerning, because younger patients might have more cumulative years at risk for the consequences of incomplete kidney recovery and CKD progression. Although the acute kidney injury work group clinical practice guideline ( 9 ) recommends kidney-function assessment within 3 months after AKI, national post-AKI follow-up among Medicare beneficiaries (13.6% in 2023), below the Healthy People 2030 target of 16.4% ( Objective CKD-03 )

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . Linking drug overdose–involved hospitalizations of patients with AKI to postdischarge kidney function follow-up could help identify patients at risk for persistent kidney dysfunction and support early detection and management of CKD.

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: The findings in this report are subject to at least four limitations. First, hospitals participating in PHD might differ from nonparticipating hospitals in urbanicity, hospital size, or overdose incidence, which could limit generalizability. Second, analyses were conducted at the hospitalization level and did not account for within-patient correlation, which could have underestimated SEs. Third, AKI was identified using diagnosis codes rather than laboratory-based criteria, which might have resulted in an underestimate of AKI occurrence. In addition, although certain underlying medical conditions potentially associated with AKI such as diabetes and heart disease were accounted for, not all relevant conditions were assessed

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . Information on intensive care unit admission and duration of hospitalization was not assessed; therefore, whether these factors might have contributed to the development of AKI or a severe hospital course could not be determined. Finally, selected diagnosis-code categories limited assessment of combinations, adulterants, dose, route, duration, exposure timing, and other drug classes with potential AKI relevance. In addition, expanded availability of naloxone, a medication that reverses opioid overdose since 2019, might have affected which opioid-involved overdose events resulted in hospitalization ( 10 ).

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: This study assessed national trends in AKI and AKI-related severe inpatient courses among drug overdose–involved hospitalizations across a broad range of real-world hospitalization settings. Public health efforts focusing on preventing drug overdose to reduce subsequent AKI risk, promoting early recognition of kidney injury, and improving continuity of kidney care after hospitalization might reduce the occurrence of drug overdose–involved AKI. Strategies might include expanding overdose prevention measures, such as naloxone distribution and substance use treatment access, encouraging timely medical evaluation for suspected drug overdose, and improving clinician awareness of AKI risk among patients with a drug overdose

title: CDC: Acute Kidney Injury Among Patients with Drug Overdose–Involved Hospitalizations — United States, 2016–2025
text: . Linking patients with AKI to postdischarge kidney follow-up care and substance use treatment services to prevent future drug overdoses and recurrent AKI could support long-term kidney health, particularly among younger patients who were more likely to have a severe inpatient course and might have more future years at risk for cumulative kidney consequences after AKI. In addition, because females experienced a higher percentage of severe inpatient outcomes despite a lower overall percentage of AKI, clinicians might consider monitoring female patients hospitalized for drug overdose for signs of severe complications, especially when AKI occurs.

title: CDC: Symptoms of Dengue and Testing
text:
## Symptoms of Dengue and Testing
## Key points
- 1 in 4: About one in four people infected with dengue will get sick.
- For people who get sick with dengue, symptoms can be mild or severe.
- Severe dengue can be life-threatening within a few hours and often requires care at a hospital.
## Symptoms
The most common symptom of dengue is fever with any of the following:
- Aches and pains (headache, eye pain, typically behind the eyes, muscle, joint, or bone pain)
- Nausea, vomiting
- Rash
- Any warning sign
- Mild symptoms of dengue can be confused with other illnesses that cause fever.
- Symptoms of dengue typically last 2–7 days.
- Most people will recover after about a week.

title: CDC: Symptoms of Dengue and Testing
text:
## When to seek emergency help
Symptoms of dengue can become severe within a few hours. Severe dengue is a medical emergency.
About 1 in 20 people who get sick with dengue will develop severe dengue. Severe dengue can result in shock, internal bleeding, and death.
Warning signs are symptoms that indicate a person may be at higher risk for developing severe dengue. Immediately go to a local clinic or emergency room if you or a family member has any of the following warning signs:
- Belly pain or tenderness
- Vomiting (at least 3 times in 24 hours)
- Bleeding from the nose or gums
- Vomiting blood, or blood in the stool
- Feeling extremely tired or restless
## Warning Signs

title: CDC: Symptoms of Dengue and Testing
text:

## Testing
- See your healthcare provider if you have symptoms of dengue and live in or have recently traveled to an area with risk of dengue .
- A blood test is the only way to confirm the diagnosis. Laboratory confirmation is not required to manage illness from dengue, and your healthcare provider might provide care based on your signs and symptoms.

title: CDC: Plague Maps and Statistics
text:
## Plague Maps and Statistics
## Key points
- An average of five human plague cases are reported each year in the United States.
- Plague occurs in the western United States, with most cases in northern New Mexico and Arizona.
- More recent plague epidemics have occurred in Africa, Asia, and South America, but most human cases since the 1990s have occurred in Africa.

title: CDC: Plague Maps and Statistics
text:
## Plague in the United States
Plague was first introduced into the United States in 1900, from rat–infested steamships that had sailed from affected areas. Epidemics occurred in port cities. The last urban plague epidemic in the United States occurred in Los Angeles from 1924 through 1925. Plague then spread from urban rats to rural rodent species and became entrenched in many areas of the western United States. Since that time, plague has occurred as scattered cases in rural areas. Most human cases in the United States are acquired in two regions:
- Northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, and southern Colorado
- California, southern Oregon, and far western Nevada

title: CDC: Plague Maps and Statistics
text:
## Quick facts
- Over 80% of United States plague cases have been the bubonic form .
- In recent decades, an average of five human plague cases have been reported each year (range: 0–17 cases per year).
- Plague has occurred in people of all ages (infants up to age 96), though 50% of cases occur in people ages 12–45.
- Plague occurs in both men and women, though historically is slightly more common among men, probably because of increased outdoor activities that put them at higher risk.
## Reported cases in humans
Since the mid–20th century, plague in the United States has typically occurred in the rural West. Cases in the eastern United States are among people who traveled from the west or from laboratory exposure.

## Plague worldwide
More recent plague epidemics have occurred in Africa, Asia, and South America, but most human cases since the 1990s have occurred in Africa. Almost all cases reported in the last 20 years have occurred among people living in small towns and villages or agricultural areas, rather than in larger towns and cities.

title: CDC: Adult Obesity Prevalence Maps
text:
## Adult Obesity Prevalence Maps
## What to know
## Overview
The CDC 2025 Adult Obesity Prevalence Maps for 47 states, the District of Columbia (DC), Guam, and Puerto Rico show the proportion of adults with a body mass index (BMI) greater than or equal to 30 kg/m 2 based on self-reported weight and height. Data are presented by location, age, education level, and race and ethnicity. The data come from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System , an ongoing state-based, telephone interview survey conducted by CDC and state health departments.
The 2025 maps show that obesity impacts some groups more than others. There are notable differences by individual characteristics, including by location, age, education level, and race and ethnicity.
See adult BMI categories .

title: CDC: Adult Obesity Prevalence Maps
text:
## Keep in Mind
Preventing and treating obesity is important for health and well-being. These new data highlight the need for obesity prevention and treatment efforts from childhood into adulthood. This includes providing access to and promoting healthy foods, safe places for physical activity, and evidence-based health care services including lifestyle interventions and FDA-approved medications.
Read more about what can be done .

title: CDC: Adult Obesity Prevalence Maps
text:
## By location across states and territories
In 2025, among U.S. states and territories with available data, all had an obesity prevalence higher than 25%, except the District of Columbia (24.2%). Overall, the Midwest (35.5%) and South (34.8%) had the highest prevalence of obesity, followed by the West (30.7%) and the Northeast (29.6%).
- One jurisdiction (District of Columbia) had an obesity prevalence between 20% and less than 25%.
- 7 states had an obesity prevalence between 25% and less than 30%.
- 19 states had an obesity prevalence between 30% and less than 35%.
- 21 states, Guam, and Puerto Rico had an obesity prevalence between 35% and less than 40%.
- No state or territory had an obesity prevalence of 40% or higher.

title: CDC: Adult Obesity Prevalence Maps
text:
- No state or territory had an obesity prevalence of 40% or higher.
In 2025, the prevalence of adult obesity varied by age. Middle-aged adults (40–59 years) are about 36% more likely to have obesity than younger adults (18–39 years) and 25% more likely to have obesity than older adults (60 and older). Among U.S. states and territories with available data, the number with an obesity prevalence of 35% or higher is:
- 6 states and 1 territory among adults 18–39 years.
- 40 states and 2 territories among adults 40–59 years.
- 11 states and 1 territory among adults 60 years and older.
In 2025, among U.S. states and territories with available data, obesity prevalence was highest among adults without a high school diploma or equivalent (38.1%) and lowest among college graduates (27.8%).
- 38.1% of adults without a high school diploma or equivalent had obesity.

title: CDC: Adult Obesity Prevalence Maps
text:
- 38.1% of adults without a high school diploma or equivalent had obesity.
- 35.1% of adults with a high school diploma or equivalent had obesity.
- 36.8% of adults with some college education had obesity.
- 27.8% of college graduates had obesity.
Combined BRFSS data from 2023–2025 show notable differences in adult obesity prevalence by race and ethnicity. Among states, territories, or DC with enough data, the number with an obesity prevalence of 35% or higher is:
- Asian adults: 0 (among 35 states, 1 territory, and DC)
- White adults: 13 (among 44 states, 2 territories, and DC)
- Hispanic adults: 32 (among 44 states, 2 territories, and DC)
- Black adults: 35 (among 44 states and DC)

title: CDC: Current Research Projects
text:
## Current Research Projects
## What to know
The Division of Diabetes Translation (DDT) conducts and supports studies, often in collaboration with partners, to develop and apply sound science to reduce the burden of diabetes. These studies also help to address the research needs of DDT programs and the diabetes community.
## Applied research and surveillance
Applied research includes studies to:
- Identify risk factors that can change.
- Determine the effectiveness of interventions at the individual, health care system, community, and policy levels.
- Prioritize the value of successful interventions.
Surveillance involves the collection and analysis of data to:
- Identify the burden and magnitude of diabetes and its related conditions.
- Evaluate the impact of diabetes prevention programs.
- Guide decision-making.
- Prioritize national public health objectives.

title: CDC: Current Research Projects
text:
## Current projects
- Diabetes in Young Adults (DiYA) Study – The DiYA study assesses new cases of type 1 and type 2 diabetes in young adults (aged 20–45 years) using data from Kaiser Permanente in California. Although half of the cases of type 1 diabetes occur in adulthood, there are very limited data on the incidence of type 1 diabetes in the U.S. adult population.
- Assessing the Burden of Diabetes by Type in Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults (DiCAYA) Study – The DiCAYA study is a multicenter collaboration that seeks to capitalize on electronic health record data to modernize diabetes surveillance efforts and monitor trends in diabetes prevalence and incidence by diabetes type.

title: CDC: Current Research Projects
text:
## Health policy and health services
Health policy and health services research examines the effect of health policies and system-based approaches on the risks and outcomes of diabetes for various population groups.
## Current projects
Natural Experiments for Translation in Diabetes 3.0 (NEXT-D3) Study – The NEXT-D3 Network is a 5-year research collaboration to evaluate the impacts of naturally occurring policies and practice changes, with a focus on diabetes-related outcomes.
NEXT-D3 projects address:
- Whether and to what extent federal or state legislative policies and health plan innovations affect type 2 diabetes risk and diabetes treatment and outcomes.
- The real-world effects of increased access to health insurance under the Affordable Care Act.
- The effectiveness of interventions that reduce barriers to medication access.

title: CDC: Current Research Projects
text:
## Effectiveness research
Effectiveness research assesses whether interventions and strategies to prevent, diagnose, treat, and monitor diabetes work. This research is designed to identify for patients, health care providers, and decision makers the interventions or strategies that are most effective for specific populations under certain circumstances.

title: CDC: Current Research Projects
text:
## Current projects
- Action for Health in Diabetes (Look AHEAD)-Extension – The Look AHEAD-Extension study assesses the long-term effect of an intensive lifestyle intervention on life expectancy, health care costs, and key dimensions of healthy aging (less frailty, reduced small blood vessel complications from diabetes, and improved quality of life).
- 30-Year Follow-up of Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Study – This study examines the long-term effects of lifestyle changes on major cardiovascular disease, microvascular (small blood vessel) complications (such as eye and kidney diseases), and life expectancy.

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## Type 1 Diabetes
## Key points
- With type 1 diabetes, your pancreas doesn't make insulin or makes very little insulin.
- People with type 1 diabetes need to take insulin every day.
- Currently, type 1 diabetes can't be prevented, but it can be treated effectively.

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## What is type 1 diabetes?
If you have type 1 diabetes, your pancreas doesn't make insulin or makes very little insulin. Insulin helps blood sugar enter the cells in your body for use as energy.
Without insulin, blood sugar can't get into cells and builds up in the bloodstream. High blood sugar is damaging to the body and causes many of the symptoms and complications of diabetes.
Type 1 diabetes was once called insulin-dependent or juvenile diabetes. It often develops in children, teens, and young adults, but it can happen at any age.
Type 1 diabetes is less common than type 2 —about 5-10% of people with diabetes have type 1. Currently, no one knows how to prevent type 1 diabetes, but it can be managed successfully by:
- Following your doctor's recommendations for living a healthy lifestyle.
- Managing your blood sugar.
- Getting regular health checkups.

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## Signs and symptoms
People with type 1 diabetes in its early stages don't have any symptoms. As type 1 progresses, symptoms can appear suddenly, in just a few weeks or months, and can be severe.
Some type 1 diabetes symptoms are similar to symptoms of other health conditions. Don't guess! If you think you could have type 1 diabetes, see your doctor to get your blood sugar tested. Untreated diabetes can lead to very serious—even fatal—health problems.

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## Risk factors
Risk factors for type 1 diabetes are not as clear as for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. Known risk factors include:
- Family history : Having a parent, brother, or sister with type 1 diabetes.
- Age : You can get type 1 diabetes at any age, but it usually develops in children, teens, or young adults.
In the United States, White people are more likely to develop type 1 diabetes than African American and Hispanic or Latino people.

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## Causes
Type 1 diabetes is thought to be caused by an autoimmune reaction (the body attacks itself by mistake). This reaction destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin, called beta cells. This process can go on for months or years before any symptoms appear.
Some people have certain genes (traits passed on from parent to child) that increase their chance of developing type 1 diabetes. However, many of them won't go on to have type 1 diabetes even if they have the genes. A trigger in the environment, such as a virus, may also play a part in developing type 1 diabetes. Diet and lifestyle habits don't cause type 1 diabetes.

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## Testing and screening
A simple blood test is used to screen for diabetes. If you were tested at a health fair or pharmacy, follow up at a clinic or doctor's office. That way you'll be sure the results are accurate.
If your doctor thinks you have type 1 diabetes or are at high risk for type 1, you may also be screened for diabetes-related autoantibodies . This can detect early stages of type 1 diabetes, which can be treated before symptoms and serious complications appear. In addition to autoantibody testing, your doctor may have your urine tested for ketones. Ketones are produced when your body burns fat for energy. Having ketones in your urine may indicate you have type 1 diabetes instead of type 2.
## Screening at a glance

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## Screening at a glance
## Treatment
Unlike many health conditions, diabetes is managed mostly by you, with support from your health care team:
- Primary care doctor
- Foot doctor
- Dentist
- Eye doctor
- Registered dietitian nutritionist
- Diabetes educator
- Pharmacist
Also ask your family, teachers, and other important people in your life for help and support. Managing diabetes can be challenging, but everything you do to improve your health is worth it!

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
## For parents
You'll need to take insulin shots (or wear an insulin pump) every day. Insulin is needed to manage your blood sugar levels and give your body energy. You can't take insulin as a pill. That's because the acid in your stomach would destroy it before it could get into your bloodstream. Your doctor will work with you to figure out the most effective type and dosage of insulin for you.
You'll also need to do regular blood sugar checks . Ask your doctor how often you should check it and what your target blood sugar levels should be. Keeping your blood sugar levels as close to target as possible will help you prevent or delay diabetes-related complications .
Hypoglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis are common complications of diabetes, and you'll need to know how to handle them. Meet with your doctor for step-by-step instructions.

title: CDC: Type 1 Diabetes
text:
Stress is a part of life, but it can make managing diabetes harder. Regular physical activity, getting enough sleep, and exercises to relax can help. Talk to your doctor and diabetes educator about these and other ways you can manage stress.
Healthy lifestyle habits are really important too:
- Making healthy food choices
- Being physically active
- Managing your blood pressure
- Managing your cholesterol
Regular appointments with your health care team can help you stay on track with your treatment plan and offer new ideas and strategies if needed.

title: CDC: 10 Surprising Things That Can Spike Your Blood Sugar
text:
## 10 Surprising Things That Can Spike Your Blood Sugar
## What to know
If you have managed your diabetes for a while, you have seen how food, activity, stress, and illness can affect your blood sugar levels. But there are things that trigger blood sugar spikes that you may find surprising.

title: CDC: 10 Surprising Things That Can Spike Your Blood Sugar
text:
## Do you know all these blood sugar triggers?
- Sunburn —the pain causes stress, and stress increases blood sugar levels.
- Artificial sweeteners—some studies show they can raise blood sugar.
- Coffee—even without sweetener. Some people's blood sugar is extra-sensitive to caffeine.
- Losing sleep—even just one night of too little sleep can make your body use insulin less efficiently.
- Skipping breakfast—going without that morning meal can increase blood sugar after both lunch and dinner.
- Time of day—blood sugar can be harder to control the later it gets.
- Dawn phenomenon—hormones tend to surge early in the morning, and for people with diabetes blood sugar can spike.
- Dehydration—less water in your body means that your blood sugar is more concentrated.
- Nose spray—some contain chemicals that trigger your liver to make more blood sugar.

title: CDC: 10 Surprising Things That Can Spike Your Blood Sugar
text:
- Nose spray—some contain chemicals that trigger your liver to make more blood sugar.
- Gum disease —it's both a blood sugar spiker and a complication of diabetes.
Individual responses to each of these triggers may vary. If an activity or food is new, check your blood sugar before and after to see how you respond.

title: CDC: Preventing High Cholesterol
text:
## Preventing High Cholesterol
## Key points
- By living a healthy lifestyle, you can help keep your cholesterol in a healthy range.
- Overweight and obesity raise levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL or “bad”) cholesterol.

title: CDC: Preventing High Cholesterol
text:
## Make healthy eating choices
Your body makes all of the cholesterol it needs, so you do not need to obtain cholesterol through foods. Eating lots of foods high in saturated fat and trans fat may contribute to high cholesterol and related conditions, such as heart disease.
What you can do to help prevent cholesterol:
Limit foods high in saturated fat. Saturated fats come from animal products (such as cheese, fatty meats, and dairy desserts) and tropical oils (such as palm oil). Foods that are higher in saturated fat may be high in cholesterol.
Choose foods that are low in saturated fat, trans fat, sodium (salt), and added sugars. These foods include lean meats; seafood; fat-free or low-fat milk, cheese, and yogurt; whole grains; and fruits and vegetables.

title: CDC: Preventing High Cholesterol
text:
Eat foods naturally high in fiber, such as oatmeal and beans (black, pinto, kidney, lima, and others), and unsaturated fats (found in avocados, vegetable oils like olive oil, and nuts). These foods may help prevent and manage high levels of LDL ("bad") cholesterol and triglycerides while increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL, or "good") cholesterol levels.
Find healthy, seasonal recipes at the Million Hearts ® healthy recipes page .

title: CDC: Preventing High Cholesterol
text:
## Prevention steps and strategies
## Maintain a healthy weight
Overweight and obesity raise levels of LDL ("bad") cholesterol. Excess body fat affects how your body uses cholesterol and slows down your body's ability to remove LDL cholesterol from your blood. The combination raises your risk of heart disease and stroke.
What you can do:
To determine whether your weight is in a healthy range, doctors often calculate your body mass index (BMI). If you know your weight and height, you can calculate your BMI at CDC's Assessing Your Weight website . Doctors sometimes also use waist and hip measurements to measure excess body fat.
Talk with your doctor about what a healthy weight is for you. Work with your doctor on a food and fitness plan to help you reach or maintain a healthy weight.

title: CDC: Preventing High Cholesterol
text:
## Get regular physical activity
Physical activity can help you maintain a healthy weight and lower your cholesterol and blood pressure levels.
What you can do:
Get active as a family. For adults, the Surgeon General recommends 2 hours and 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise, such as brisk walking or bicycling, every week. Children and adolescents should get 1 hour of physical activity every day.
Make physical activity a part of each day. Take the stairs instead of the elevator, park a little farther away, walk to the store, or do jumping jacks during commercials.

title: CDC: Preventing High Cholesterol
text:
## Quit smoking
Smoking damages your blood vessels, speeds up the hardening of the arteries, and greatly increases your risk for heart disease. If you don't smoke, don't start. If you do smoke, quitting will lower your risk for heart disease.
What you can do:
- Talk with your doctor about ways to help you quit.
- Learn more about tobacco use and ways to quit at CDC's Smoking and Tobacco Use website .
## Limit alcohol
Too much alcohol can raise cholesterol levels and levels of triglycerides , a type of fat in the blood.
What you can do:
- Avoid drinking too much alcohol. Men should have no more than two drinks per day, and women should have no more than one.
- Learn more at CDC's Alcohol and Public Health website .

title: CDC: Preventing High Cholesterol
text:
## Work with your health care team
You and your health care team can work together to prevent high cholesterol. Discuss your other medical conditions and any medicines you are taking, and bring a list of questions to your appointments. You can use this list of questions from the Million Hearts ® The Scoop on Statins web page .
